section: Cost and Efficiency: The Economics of Storage
title: Storage is the bill that grows even when you do nothing
body: Most tech costs shrink when you stop using them: shut down a server and its compute charge disappears. Storage is different. Data you stop using stays on disk, and you keep paying for it every month, so storage cost only goes up by itself. At a company holding exabytes, a 10% efficiency gain is worth tens of millions of dollars per year. That is why storage efficiency is treated as a first-class engineering problem, not an accounting afterthought.
deeper:
The largest storage papers in the industry, such as Meta's f4 and Tectonic and Microsoft's Azure Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC), are as much about money as about engineering. Each one exists largely because shaving overhead off exabytes of data translates directly into huge savings.

This chapter walks through the economics in order: what a usable terabyte really costs once you count everything, how cloud providers turn those costs into a bill, which levers actually reduce cost (with real numbers where companies published them), when owning hardware beats renting it from a cloud, and how large companies run storage cost as an ongoing discipline called FinOps. It closes with the energy side of storage and a playbook that ranks levers by saving, effort and risk.

The mindset to take away: every stored byte is a recurring liability. Decisions such as how many copies to keep, which drive to buy, or whether to set an expiry date look small at design time but compound every month for years.

quiz.q: Why does storage cost tend to rise on its own while compute cost does not?
quiz.a: Compute you stop using goes away, but data you stop using stays stored and keeps being billed every month unless someone actively deletes it.

title: A $15 hard drive is only one line of a six-line bill
body: Saying 'a hard drive costs about $15 per TB' describes just one part of the cost. The real cost of a usable, durable, served terabyte has six parts: media (the drives), servers (chassis, CPU, RAM, network cards), redundancy overhead (replicas or parity), power and cooling, datacenter space and network, and people and software. The full number is called total cost of ownership (TCO): the cost of owning and operating something over its whole life, not just its purchase price.
deeper:
Each part behaves differently. Media cost falls steadily over the years. Server cost depends on how many drives each machine carries. Redundancy overhead multiplies both media and servers: 3x replication triples them, while erasure coding cuts the multiplier to about 1.3x to 1.7x. Power and cooling are paid every hour for drives, CPUs and fans, with cooling adding more on top. Datacenter space and network cover racks, floor space, top-of-rack switches and the bandwidth needed to read the data back. People and software include engineers who build and run the system, on-call duty, hardware replacement and software licenses.

The practical consequence is that comparing options by drive price alone is misleading. A design that uses cheaper drives but needs more copies, more servers or more operators can easily cost more in TCO. When evaluating any storage plan, list all six lines, even if some are rough estimates, before declaring one option cheaper than another.

quiz.q: Why is quoting the drive price per TB a poor estimate of what storage really costs?
quiz.a: Drives are only media. TCO also includes servers, redundancy overhead, power and cooling, datacenter space and network, and people and software over the system's whole life.

title: Hard drive prices fell about 8x from 2009 to 2022
body: Media is the drives themselves. Backblaze, a company that publishes its hard drive costs, reported about $0.014 per GB (about $14 per TB) for 16 TB drives in late 2022, down from $0.114 per GB in 2009. That steady fall is why raw disk now looks almost free per terabyte. Flash storage (SSDs) costs several times more per TB than hard disk drives (HDDs), so the choice of media still matters a lot for the total bill.
deeper:
Backblaze is a useful reference because few companies publish their actual purchase costs; most big players treat hardware pricing as secret. Its figures show the long-run trend: roughly an eightfold drop in cost per GB over about thirteen years.

But cheap media does not make storage cheap. Because drive prices dropped so far, media has become a minority of the total cost of a usable terabyte. The other lines, such as servers, redundancy, fill headroom, power, space and people, now dominate. A team that focuses only on buying cheaper drives will miss the larger multipliers.

The flash versus HDD gap is also important. Flash costs several times more per TB, but it delivers vastly more IOPS (input/output operations per second) per TB. Later in the chapter this becomes a decision rule: pick HDD for data that is limited by capacity and flash for data limited by IOPS, because the cheapest medium per TB is not always the cheapest medium for the workload.

quiz.q: If drive prices have fallen so much, why hasn't total storage cost fallen by the same factor?
quiz.a: Media is now a minority of TCO. Servers, redundancy, fill headroom, power, space, network and people make up most of the cost and did not fall with drive prices.

title: Dropbox packed 100 disks into a box built for 60
body: Drives cannot work alone: they need a server chassis, CPU, memory and network cards. That server cost is shared across every drive in the machine, so denser servers spread it over more terabytes and lower the cost per TB. Dropbox's 2018 SMR storage design went from 60 to 100 disks per machine while keeping the same CPU and memory. The server share of each terabyte fell because the same compute now served far more disks.
deeper:
Server density is a quiet but powerful lever. If a server with a fixed CPU, RAM and network budget can host 100 drives instead of 60, the server cost per drive falls by about 40%. For cold or warm data, where a single CPU can keep up with many slow drives, there is little reason to pay for extra compute.

The limit is performance. More drives per server means more data behind each network card and each CPU, and longer rebuilds when a whole machine fails. That is acceptable for large, mostly immutable blobs like Dropbox's, but a hot database with heavy random reads would saturate the CPU or network long before the disks fill.

Dropbox's design paired this density with SMR (shingled magnetic recording) drives, which fit more data per drive, and an SSD cache to absorb writes. Together these changes are discussed later in the chapter, where Dropbox reports saving more than 20% overall versus its previous storage generation.

quiz.q: Why does putting more disks behind the same CPU and memory reduce cost per TB, and when does it stop working?
quiz.a: Fixed server cost is spread over more terabytes. It stops working when CPU, network or rebuild time become bottlenecks, as with hot random-access workloads.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
title: Price usable TB, not raw TB: a $15 drive becomes $39.40
body: A common trap is pricing raw capacity when users actually consume usable capacity. A teaching example (assumed numbers, not a real company): start with media at $15 per raw TB. Add servers at about 50% more: $22.50. Keep 20% free for growth and rebuilds, so divide by 0.8: $28.10. Multiply by erasure coding overhead of 1.4x (like RS(10,4)): $39.40 per usable TB. Spread over a 5-year drive life of 60 months: about $0.66 per usable TB-month for hardware.
deeper:
Each step is a multiplier, and multipliers compound. The fill target matters because a storage cluster can never run at 100%: you need free space for growth before new hardware arrives and for rebuilding data when drives fail. Running at 80% full means every stored byte carries 25% extra hardware.

The redundancy step is the biggest single multiplier. RS(10,4) splits data into 10 pieces plus 4 parity pieces, so 14 units of disk hold 10 units of data, a 1.4x overhead.

The lifetime step converts a purchase into a monthly cost. A longer drive life lowers monthly cost, but older drives fail more and are less dense, so lifetime is itself a trade-off.

Note that this $0.66 figure covers hardware only. Power, space, network and people come on top, and the chapter warns they often equal or exceed the hardware line. The point of the exercise is structural, not the specific dollar figures.

quiz.q: In the raw-to-usable calculation, why do you divide by the fill target?
quiz.a: Clusters must keep free space (here 20%) for growth and rebuilds, so each usable byte needs extra purchased capacity; dividing by 0.8 adds that hidden cost.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
title: Choosing 3x replication over EC more than doubles hardware cost
body: Rerun the usable-TB example with 3x replication instead of 1.4x erasure coding and the hardware cost rises from about $0.66 to about $1.40 per usable TB-month. The redundancy choice alone more than doubles hardware cost. On top of hardware come power, space, network and people, which often equal or exceed the hardware line. The lesson is structural: media is a minority of the cost, while redundancy, fill level and lifetime multiply everything.
deeper:
The chapter deliberately does not guess the non-hardware numbers, because power, space, network and staffing costs are private at every big company. What it does show is where leverage lives.

Since redundancy multiplies both media and servers, a change in scheme ripples through the whole hardware line. Going from 3.0x to 1.4x shrinks physical bytes by more than half for the same user data. Fill level and drive lifetime act the same way: small changes in each produce proportional changes in the total.

This is also why the biggest industry storage papers focus on redundancy. Meta's f4 cut its effective replication factor from 3.6 to 2.1, and Azure's LRC reached about 1.33x, because at exabyte scale that single multiplier dwarfs any saving from haggling over drive prices.

A useful habit: when someone proposes a storage design, identify its redundancy factor, fill target and assumed lifetime first. Those three numbers tell you more about its cost than the drive model does.

quiz.q: Why does changing the redundancy scheme have more effect on cost than negotiating a cheaper drive price?
quiz.a: Redundancy multiplies both media and server cost; moving from 3x to 1.4x more than halves physical bytes, while drive price affects only the minority media line.

section: 12.1.1 From raw TB to usable TB
title: Four questions that expose a 5x gap in cost-per-TB claims
body: Senior staff lens: whenever someone quotes a cost per TB, ask four questions. Is it raw or usable capacity? Which redundancy scheme does it assume? What fill level? Does it include power, space and people? Two teams can be off by 5 times just from these assumptions, even when both are honest and use the same hardware. Pinning down these assumptions is the first step in any serious storage cost discussion or comparison between systems.
deeper:
The 5x spread comes from multiplying assumptions. Raw versus usable can differ by the redundancy factor, anywhere from about 1.33x to 3x or more. A cluster run at 50% full costs 1.6 times as much per stored byte as one at 80%. Including power, space, network and people can roughly double the hardware-only figure. Stack these and a factor of five is easy.

The chapter's quiz answer adds a fifth assumption worth checking: drive lifetime. Amortizing hardware over three years versus five changes the monthly cost by about two-thirds.

In practice, this lens prevents bad decisions such as comparing a cloud list price (which includes everything plus margin) against the raw price of drives, or crediting one internal team with 'cheaper storage' when it simply runs at higher fill or counts fewer copies. Before debating whose system is cheaper, normalize everyone to usable, durable TB with the same scope of included costs.

quiz.q: Two teams report very different cost per TB for the same hardware. What four assumptions should you check first?
quiz.a: Raw vs usable capacity, the redundancy scheme, the fill level, and whether power, space, network and people are included (drive lifetime is another).

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
title: A cloud storage bill has five lines, not one
body: Cloud providers turn their TCO into a price list. A cloud storage bill has five main parts: storage (GB stored per month), requests (a fee for each API call), retrieval (a per-GB fee for reading from cool storage classes), egress (data leaving the region to the internet), and replication and transfer (copies to other regions and traffic between zones). Using Amazon S3 in US East as the example, each line has its own price, and any of them can dominate.
deeper:
The chapter uses S3 US East list prices checked in 2026. Storage for S3 Standard is $0.023 per GB-month for the first 50 TB, falling to $0.021 above 500 TB. Requests are split by type: PUT, COPY, POST and LIST cost $0.005 per 1,000, while GET costs $0.0004 per 1,000. Retrieval is charged per GB for the Infrequent Access (IA) and Glacier classes, which trade lower storage price for a fee when you read. Egress to the internet is $0.09 per GB for the first tier, with the first 10 GB per month free. Replication and transfer are charged per GB transferred, plus the storage of the replica.

Engineers usually think only about the storage line because it maps to disk space. But the other four lines follow access patterns, not size. A design with many small writes, frequent reads from cold tiers, heavy internet serving or cross-region copies can have a bill shaped very differently from what the stored gigabytes suggest.

quiz.q: Why can two workloads storing the same number of GB have very different cloud bills?
quiz.a: Only one line depends on bytes stored; requests, retrieval, egress and transfer depend on access patterns such as write count, cold reads, internet serving and replication.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
title: On S3, a PUT costs 12.5 times more than a GET
body: S3 charges $0.005 per 1,000 PUT, COPY, POST or LIST requests but only $0.0004 per 1,000 GETs, so a write request costs 12.5 times more than a read. This surprises engineers because requests feel free. For a workload that writes billions of tiny objects, request charges can exceed the cost of storing the data. The object size is the key: small objects mean many requests per gigabyte, while the storage charge stays tied to total bytes.
deeper:
Consider the arithmetic. One million PUTs cost $5. If each object is 1 KB, those million objects total about 1 GB, which costs roughly two cents per month to store in S3 Standard. The requests cost hundreds of times more than a month of storage. With large objects, say 2 MB photos, the balance flips and storage dominates.

This pricing pushes designs toward fewer, larger objects. Batching small records into bigger files, as log pipelines and lake tables do, cuts request counts dramatically. Compaction, listed later in the playbook, serves the same purpose for streaming lake tables: it merges many small files into fewer large ones, reducing request charges and improving compression, at the cost of some write amplification.

LIST calls are priced like PUTs, so designs that repeatedly list large prefixes to find new data can also run up surprising request bills.

quiz.q: Why can request charges exceed storage charges for some workloads on S3?
quiz.a: Requests are billed per call regardless of size. Billions of tiny objects mean huge request counts while total bytes stay small, especially since PUTs cost 12.5 times GETs.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
title: Serving a GB once costs about four months of storing it
body: Egress is data leaving a cloud region to the internet. S3 charges $0.09 per GB for the first tier, after the first free 10 GB per month. Storing that same GB in S3 Standard costs roughly $0.023 per month, so sending it out once costs about four times more than keeping it for a month. For media-heavy apps this line can dominate. That is why companies put a CDN (content delivery network) in front of object storage to absorb most reads.
deeper:
A CDN caches popular content at edge locations near users. When a user loads a photo, the CDN serves it from its cache; only cache misses go back to the origin bucket. That reduces both egress and GET request charges on the storage side. Companies also negotiate volume discounts, which is why the chapter's worked example assumes a blended $0.05 per GB rather than the $0.09 list price.

The chapter's quiz makes the point sharper: for a video streaming service serving many petabytes per month to the internet, egress would dominate the bill instead of storage, unless a CDN or peering deal absorbs it.

Egress also shapes the cloud versus on-prem decision. Heavy egress to users or partners is listed as a factor that favors owning infrastructure, because on-prem bandwidth is typically bought as capacity rather than billed per GB. The playbook rates 'reduce egress with CDN' as a large saving for media, with cache misses as the main risk.

quiz.q: Why do companies place a CDN in front of object storage?
quiz.a: Internet egress is expensive (about $0.09 per GB, roughly four months of storage). A CDN serves most reads from its cache, cutting origin egress and request charges.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
title: AWS bills your own cross-zone replication traffic
body: S3 replicates data across Availability Zones (separate datacenters within a region) and includes that in its price. But if you run your own replicated database or Kafka on virtual machines across three zones, AWS bills the data transfer between zones. AWS's architecture blog notes that traffic crossing an Availability Zone boundary typically incurs a charge, while traffic within one zone is free. At the time of writing, the common EC2 list rate is about $0.01 per GB in each direction.
deeper:
This is the line engineers most often miss because it does not show up as storage at all. It appears as data transfer on the compute side of the bill, far from the database team's mental model of disk cost.

The mechanism: a self-managed database spread across three zones for fault tolerance sends every write to replicas in the other two zones. Each of those transfers is billed on both ends, at about $0.01 per GB out and $0.01 per GB in. So each replicated byte effectively costs $0.02 per destination zone. Multiply by write volume and it adds up fast.

The chapter notes the rate should be verified before use, since prices change. The trade-off is real: keeping replicas in one zone avoids the charge but loses zone isolation, so an outage of that zone could take down the whole database. The playbook lists 'avoid cross-zone chatter' as a lever whose saving can exceed disk cost, with lower zone isolation as its risk.

quiz.q: Why does a self-managed 3-zone database incur transfer charges when S3 data replicated across zones does not?
quiz.a: S3 includes its internal cross-zone replication in its price, but traffic you generate between VMs in different zones is billed, about $0.01 per GB each direction.

section: 12.2 Anatomy of a cloud storage bill
title: Common mistake: the forgotten 3-zone replication bill
body: A common mistake is designing a self-managed database across three Availability Zones and forgetting the replication traffic in the cost estimate. Each byte written is copied to two other zones, and each of those transfers is billed on both ends, leaving and entering. For a write-heavy system, such as the chapter's running example message store, this transfer line can be larger than the cost of the disks holding the data. Estimates that price only storage volume miss it completely.
deeper:
Why it can exceed disk cost: disk is billed once per stored GB per month, but transfer is billed on every byte written, including updates, rewrites and compactions that never grow the stored size. A write-heavy workload may rewrite its data many times per month, so transfer scales with churn rather than size.

In the chapter's worked bill, the messages database writes 100 TB per month, copied to 2 other zones at $0.02 round-trip per GB, adding about $4,000 per month. That is small relative to a photo store's $1 million storage line, but for a database whose own disk footprint is modest it can be the dominant cost.

Mitigations include compressing replication streams, reducing write amplification, choosing a managed service whose cross-zone replication is included in its price, or accepting fewer zones where the durability requirements allow. Whatever the choice, the replication topology must be part of the cost model from day one, not discovered on the first invoice.

quiz.q: Why can cross-zone replication cost more than disk for a write-heavy database?
quiz.a: Disk is billed on stored size, but transfer is billed on every byte written times two zones, both ends. High write churn makes transfer grow far faster than stored bytes.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Pricing a 1-billion-user app: the assumptions
body: The chapter prices part of its running 1-billion-user app on S3 US East, using 2026 list prices and teaching assumptions. It stores 50 PB of photos and videos. It receives 25 million photo uploads per day, each stored in 4 sizes, giving 100 million PUTs per day (about 3 billion per month) and about 1.5 PB of growth per month at 2 MB per photo. A CDN serves most views, so S3 sees about 3 billion GETs per day.
deeper:
The remaining assumptions cover transfer. Egress of 2 PB per month flows from AWS to a third-party CDN, at an assumed blended $0.05 per GB after volume discounts. For disaster recovery, all new uploads are copied to a second region at an assumed $0.02 per GB inter-region transfer. The messages database is self-managed on virtual machines across 3 zones, with 100 TB of writes per month, each copied to 2 other zones at $0.01 per GB in each direction.

The starting point is deliberately naive: everything sits in S3 Standard, the most expensive storage class. That makes the example useful for showing which optimization matters most.

The upload math is worth checking yourself: 25 million photos times 4 sizes gives 100 million objects per day. At 2 MB total per photo across all versions, that is 50 TB per day, or about 1.5 PB per month of new data. Getting this kind of back-of-envelope right is the foundation of any cost model.

quiz.q: Why does storing each photo in 4 sizes matter for the bill beyond just extra bytes?
quiz.a: It multiplies object count and so PUT requests: 25 million photos become 100 million PUTs per day, each billed, plus more objects to transition between tiers later.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Storage was 83% of a $1.27 million monthly bill
body: With everything in S3 Standard, the monthly bill for the example app comes to about $1.27 million. Storage of 50 PB at about $0.021 per GB costs about $1,050,000. PUT requests add $15,000, GET requests $36,000, egress to the CDN $100,000, cross-region copies $30,000, and cross-zone database traffic $4,000. Storage is about 83% of the bill, which tells you where to look first when optimizing: attack the biggest line before polishing the small ones.
deeper:
The request lines are small here because objects are large (2 MB average) and a CDN absorbs most reads. With 3 billion PUTs at $0.005 per 1,000 and 90 billion GETs at $0.0004 per 1,000, requests total about $51,000, a few percent of the bill.

One line hides a trap: replica storage growth. Every month, 1.5 PB more lands in the disaster-recovery region, so replica storage grows by about $31,500 per month, every month, compounding. The first month's bill understates it; a year later, the replica line alone adds hundreds of thousands per month.

The quiz asks why storage dominates: 50 PB at about $0.021 per GB is simply far larger than the request and transfer lines at this read and write rate. For a different business, such as a video streaming service sending many petabytes a month to the internet, egress would dominate instead. The general method is always the same: build the bill line by line and let the biggest line direct your effort.

quiz.q: In the worked example, why is the cross-region replica line more dangerous than its first-month cost suggests?
quiz.a: Replica storage compounds: 1.5 PB of new uploads lands in region 2 every month, adding about $31,500 each month on top of the previous months' growth.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Photos cool fast: 10% hot, 30% warm, 60% cold
body: Earlier evidence (Chapter 7) shows photos cool within about 3 months of upload. So the chapter assumes access data shows 10% of bytes are hot, 30% are warm (read about once every few months), and 60% are cold but must still load in milliseconds when a user scrolls back. Each group can move to a cheaper S3 storage class: hot stays in Standard, warm goes to Standard-IA (Infrequent Access), and cold goes to Glacier Instant Retrieval, which still serves reads in milliseconds.
deeper:
The key constraint is latency. Cold photos are rarely viewed, but when a user scrolls back through old posts, they must appear instantly. That rules out archival classes that need minutes or hours to restore and points to Glacier Instant Retrieval, which trades a much lower storage price for a per-GB retrieval fee.

Prices in the example: Standard $0.021 per GB-month, Standard-IA $0.0125, Glacier Instant Retrieval $0.004. The cold class is about five times cheaper than Standard per GB stored.

The split must come from measured access data, not guesswork. Tiering data that turns out to be read often will generate retrieval fees that can wipe out the saving. The takeaway in the chapter stresses tiering 'by measured access' for exactly this reason. Access patterns also shift over time, so the measurement needs to be ongoing, which is one reason access-based automatic tiering exists as a separate lever.

quiz.q: Why does the example tier cold photos to Glacier Instant Retrieval rather than a deeper archive class?
quiz.a: Cold photos must still load in milliseconds when users scroll back, so the class must serve instant reads while offering a much lower storage price.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Tiering cut the storage line by more than 60%
body: After tiering, the example stores 5 PB in Standard ($105,000), 15 PB in Standard-IA ($187,500) and 30 PB in Glacier Instant Retrieval ($120,000), plus about $6,000 in retrieval fees for an assumed 300 TB read from the cooler classes. The storage subtotal is about $418,500, down from about $1.05 million per month, a saving of more than 60%. The whole bill drops from about $1.27 million to about $640,000 per month.
deeper:
Notice where the money went. The 30 PB cold tier holds 60% of the bytes but costs only $120,000, less than the 15 PB warm tier. The biggest win comes from moving the largest group of bytes to the cheapest class that still meets the latency requirement.

Retrieval fees are the counterweight. The example assumes 300 TB per month read from IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval at about $0.01 to $0.03 per GB, costing around $6,000. That is small here because cold data really is rarely read. If a batch job scanned the whole cold tier each month, retrieval fees could swamp the saving.

The playbook later summarizes lifecycle tiering as often saving more than half of storage cost for cold data, with low effort, and with risks from retrieval fees and minimum storage durations. Minimum durations mean an object deleted soon after moving to a cool class is still billed for the minimum period, so short-lived data should not be tiered.

quiz.q: What could make the tiering saving in this example disappear?
quiz.a: Frequent reads of tiered data (for example full scans) triggering retrieval fees, deleting objects before minimum storage durations, or tiny objects whose transition fees exceed the saving.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Tiering tiny objects can cost more than it saves
body: Moving objects between storage classes has a hidden one-time cost: lifecycle transitions are billed per object. In the example, 45 PB of 2 MB objects is about 22.5 billion objects. At an assumed price of a few cents per 1,000 transitions, moving them costs hundreds of thousands of dollars once, which pays back in less than a month. But 20 KB thumbnails would mean 100 times more objects, and the transition cost can exceed the saving.
deeper:
The problem is that transition fees scale with object count while savings scale with bytes. Big objects carry many bytes per transition fee; tiny objects carry few. At some object size the per-object fee outweighs years of per-byte savings.

This is why S3 Intelligent-Tiering and Google Cloud Storage Autoclass never tier objects under 128 KB, as Chapter 7 covered. Access-based tiering services also charge a per-object monitoring fee, another cost that small objects cannot justify. The playbook notes that access-based tiering has a monitoring fee and ignores small objects.

The chapter's quiz lists three situations where tiering rarely-read data is still a bad idea: when objects are tiny (per-object transition and monitoring fees exceed the saving), when data is deleted before the minimum storage duration, and when retrieval fees from occasional full scans exceed the storage saving. Always model object count, not just bytes, before turning on a lifecycle rule.

quiz.q: Why do S3 Intelligent-Tiering and GCS Autoclass skip objects under 128 KB?
quiz.a: Transition and monitoring fees are per object while savings are per byte; for tiny objects the fees can exceed what cheaper storage saves.

section: 12.3 A worked monthly bill for the running example
title: Payback period: under 3 months yes, over 12 months be wary
body: Senior staff lens: always compute the payback period of a storage optimization. Divide the one-time cost (transitions, data rewrites, engineering time) by the monthly saving. Under 3 months is an easy yes. Over 12 months needs a strong reason, because your access pattern may change before the optimization pays back. The worked tiering example pays back in under a month, which is why it is an obvious win despite costing hundreds of thousands of dollars upfront.
deeper:
Payback turns a vague 'this saves money' into a comparable number. A migration that saves $600,000 per month and costs $300,000 once pays back in two weeks. One that saves $10,000 per month but needs a year of engineering and a costly data rewrite may never pay back.

The 12-month caution reflects uncertainty. Storage decisions rest on assumptions about access patterns, object sizes and growth. Product changes, a new feature that reads old data, or a pricing change can invalidate them. The longer the payback, the more time there is for the world to shift and turn a saving into a loss.

Include all one-time costs honestly: per-object transition fees, compute to recompress or re-encode data, temporary double storage during migration, and engineering time. Omitting engineering time is the most common way to make a mediocre optimization look attractive. This habit also helps rank competing projects: sort candidate optimizations by payback period and start with the fastest.

quiz.q: Why should an optimization with a payback period over 12 months face extra scrutiny?
quiz.a: Access patterns, product behavior or prices may change before it pays back, so a long payback carries a real risk of never recovering its one-time cost.

title: Every cost lever either stores fewer bytes or cheaper bytes
body: There are only two ways to cut storage cost: store fewer bytes, or pay less per byte. Levers that store fewer bytes include deleting unused data and setting TTLs (automatic expiry), compression, deduplication, keeping fewer replicas, and erasure coding. Levers that make bytes cheaper include tiering to colder storage classes, denser drives and SMR, and choosing the right media, flash versus disk. Some levers do both at once.
deeper:
This two-branch view is a checklist for any cost review. For each dataset, ask: can any of these bytes disappear entirely, can the remaining bytes be made smaller, and can they sit on cheaper media or a cheaper class?

The branches interact. Erasure coding reduces bytes stored relative to replication but costs CPU, network and IOPS. Tiering makes bytes cheaper but adds retrieval fees and transition costs. Denser drives lower dollars per TB but reduce IOPS per TB. Compression shrinks bytes but costs CPU on every write and read.

Order matters too. Deleting data first avoids paying to compress, deduplicate or tier bytes that should not exist. Compressing before tiering means fewer bytes to transition. Many companies start with retention hygiene and compression because they need no new hardware, then move to structural platform changes like erasure coding that require significant engineering.

The following sections cover each lever in turn with real numbers where companies published them.

quiz.q: Why is it usually best to delete unneeded data before applying compression or tiering?
quiz.a: Deleting removes bytes entirely, so you avoid paying CPU, transition fees and engineering effort to optimize data that should not exist at all.

title: Erasure coding: survive losses with (k+m)/k overhead
body: Erasure coding splits data into k data pieces and adds m parity pieces computed from them. Any k of the k+m pieces can rebuild the original data, so the system tolerates losing any m pieces. Storage overhead is (k+m)/k. For example, RS(10,4), a Reed-Solomon code with 10 data and 4 parity pieces, stores 14 units for every 10 of data, a 1.4x overhead, while surviving 4 lost pieces. Plain 3x replication costs 3.0x yet survives only 2 losses.
deeper:
The comparison is striking: erasure coding gives better fault tolerance at less than half the storage. The chapter's table:

3x replication (HDFS default, Haystack): 3.0x overhead, tolerates 2 lost pieces.
RS(6,3) (HDFS 3 default EC policy): 1.5x, tolerates 3.
RS(10,4) (f4 within a datacenter, Meta cold storage): 1.4x, tolerates 4.
RS(9,6) (Tectonic long-lived data): about 1.67x, tolerates 6.
LRC(12,2,2) (Azure Storage): about 1.33x, tolerates any 3 plus many 4-failure patterns.

The choice of k and m trades overhead against resilience and repair cost. A larger k lowers overhead but means each repair must read more pieces. A larger m improves tolerance but raises overhead. Tectonic's RS(9,6) accepts a higher overhead than RS(10,4) to tolerate 6 losses for long-lived data.

The key takeaway from the chapter: moving from 3x replication to erasure coding at 1.33x to 1.67x roughly halves hardware cost, which is why it is the biggest multiplier to get right.

quiz.q: How can RS(10,4) tolerate more failures than 3x replication while using less than half the storage?
quiz.a: Any 10 of its 14 pieces rebuild the data, so it survives 4 losses at 1.4x overhead, whereas replication needs a full copy per tolerated loss (3x for 2).

title: Haystack's 3.6x: three replicas on RAID-6 disks
body: Meta's Haystack photo store kept 3 replicas of each photo, and each replica sat on RAID-6 disks, which add their own parity at about 1.2x. The effective replication factor, meaning physical bytes stored per logical byte, was therefore 3 x 1.2 = 3.6. Meta's f4 system brought warm data down to 2.8 by using RS(10,4) at 1.4x and storing it in two datacenters (1.4 x 2 = 2.8). It later went further, to 2.1.
deeper:
Effective replication factor is the honest metric because redundancy stacks across layers. A system can advertise 'three copies' while each copy hides extra parity underneath in RAID, so the true multiplier is higher than it looks. Always multiply the layers together.

Haystack was designed for hot photos that need fast reads, where full replicas make sense. But most photos cool quickly after upload, and keeping every old photo at 3.6x wasted enormous capacity. f4 was built as a warm BLOB store specifically for that cooler data.

The step to 2.8 came from replacing replicas with erasure coding inside each datacenter: RS(10,4) gives 1.4x and tolerates 4 lost pieces, protecting against disk, host and rack failures. Keeping a second full copy in another datacenter protected against losing a whole datacenter. The next card explains how f4 cut even that second copy down to reach 2.1 while still surviving a datacenter loss.

quiz.q: Why was Haystack's effective replication factor 3.6 rather than 3?
quiz.a: Each of its 3 replicas was stored on RAID-6 disks with about 1.2x parity overhead, and stacked redundancy multiplies: 3 x 1.2 = 3.6.

title: f4's XOR trick: datacenter-proof durability at 2.1x
body: To reach 2.1x, Meta's f4 places two erasure-coded volumes, each at 1.4x, in two different datacenters. A third datacenter stores the XOR of the two volumes, also at 1.4x. So three blocks of 1.4 protect two volumes: (1.4 x 2 + 1.4) / 2 = 2.1. If any one datacenter is lost, its volume can be rebuilt from the XOR plus the surviving volume. In 2014, f4 held over 65 PB of logical data and saved over 53 PB of storage.
deeper:
XOR (exclusive or) is the simplest parity: combining volume A and volume B bit by bit gives A XOR B. If A is lost, B XOR (A XOR B) recovers A. The same works in reverse for B. So one XOR volume replaces a full second copy for each of two volumes, turning 2.8x into 2.1x.

The design works because each layer covers a specific failure. RS(10,4) within each datacenter handles disk, host and rack failures locally without cross-datacenter traffic. The XOR layer handles the rare loss of an entire datacenter. The chapter highlights this as the model for right-sizing replicas: decide which failures (disk, host, rack, datacenter) each layer of redundancy covers, and avoid paying twice for the same protection.

The cost is expensive recovery after a datacenter loss: rebuilding requires reading from two other datacenters across the wide-area network. For warm data that is rarely read, that trade is well worth the capacity saved.

quiz.q: How does f4 survive losing a whole datacenter while storing only 2.1x?
quiz.a: Two volumes sit in two datacenters and their XOR sits in a third. Any lost volume is rebuilt from the XOR plus the surviving volume, avoiding a full second copy.

title: Azure LRC and HDFS EC: cutting overhead to 1.33x and 1.5x
body: Azure Storage's Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC), which won Best Paper at USENIX ATC 2012, reach about 1.33x overhead with an LRC(12,2,2) layout. Beyond lower overhead, LRC reduces how many fragments must be read to rebuild a lost one, making repairs cheaper. On the open-source side, HDFS 3's default erasure coding policy, RS(6,3), cuts storage overhead from 200% (the extra two copies of 3x replication) to about 50%.
deeper:
LRC addresses a weakness of plain Reed-Solomon codes: repairing one lost fragment in RS(k,m) requires reading k other fragments, which is costly in network and disk. LRC adds local parities computed over smaller groups of fragments, so a common single-fragment failure can be repaired by reading only its small local group. The chapter's table notes LRC(12,2,2) tolerates any 3 failures plus many 4-failure patterns.

The HDFS figure frames overhead differently: 3x replication stores 200% extra beyond the data itself, while RS(6,3) stores 50% extra (3 parity pieces for 6 data pieces). Same idea as 3.0x versus 1.5x, just expressed as extra bytes.

These examples show erasure coding is not exotic. It is standard in major cloud storage and in open-source HDFS. The engineering work is in handling its costs: CPU, network traffic on repairs, extra IOPS for writes, and missing features, which the next card covers.

quiz.q: What problem does LRC solve beyond lowering storage overhead?
quiz.a: Plain Reed-Solomon repairs must read k fragments; LRC's local parities let a lost fragment be rebuilt from a small local group, reducing repair reads and network traffic.

title: Erasure coding's bill: CPU, network, IOPS and features
body: Erasure coding saves capacity but charges in other currencies. It needs CPU to encode on write and decode on repair. It needs network: reading a damaged or missing piece means fetching k other pieces, and HDFS notes most EC operations go off-rack, so strong network bandwidth is required. It costs IOPS, because one logical write touches k+m disks. And it can cost features: HDFS erasure-coded files do not support append or hflush.
deeper:
The IOPS cost is sharpest for small writes. Meta's Tectonic writes small appends as replicas first and re-encodes to RS(10,4) only after the block is sealed. Encoding small writes directly would take 14 IOs instead of 3, one per piece versus one per replica.

The network cost appears on every degraded read and repair. With replication, a lost copy is restored by reading one other copy. With RS(10,4), you read 10 pieces, usually from other racks. That is why rebuild network and CPU are listed as the main risk of this lever in the playbook, and why its effort is rated high: it is serious platform work.

This leads to the standard design rule in the chapter: use replication for hot, small, changing data, and erasure coding for large, sealed, cooler data. Many systems do both over an object's life, starting replicated while data is being written and read heavily, then converting to erasure coding once it is sealed and cooling.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic write small appends as replicas and only erasure-code blocks after sealing?
quiz.a: Encoding small writes directly touches all k+m disks (14 IOs instead of 3). Replicating first, then encoding sealed blocks, avoids that IOPS penalty.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
title: Bigger drives, same IOPS: the IOPS-per-TB squeeze
body: Hard drives keep getting bigger, but a drive's random IOPS (input/output operations per second) stays roughly the same, about 80 to 200, because it is limited by the mechanical arm and spinning platter. So IOPS per TB falls as drives grow. Meta's f4 used 4 TB drives with about 80 usable IOPS, or 20 IOPS per TB. A 24 TB drive with the same 80 IOPS gives only about 3.3 IOPS per TB, six times less.
deeper:
This matters whenever a workload needs a certain amount of random access per stored terabyte. Each TB of hot data generates some number of reads per second. If drives supply fewer IOPS per TB than the data demands, the drives run out of performance before they run out of space.

The result is a trap: you must buy extra drives just for their IOPS and leave their capacity empty. At that point the drive's price per TB stops mattering, because you are paying for arms, not platters. A 24 TB drive that is only 20% full costs far more per stored byte than its sticker price suggests.

The key takeaway: bigger drives reduce dollars per TB but also IOPS per TB. For cold data that is rarely read, denser drives are pure savings. For hot, random-access data, larger drives can raise the effective cost. The trap is easy to miss because drive purchasing is usually planned by capacity alone.

quiz.q: Why can buying larger hard drives increase cost for some workloads?
quiz.a: Random IOPS per drive stays flat, so IOPS per TB falls. IOPS-hungry workloads then need extra drives for performance, leaving capacity empty and raising cost per stored byte.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
title: How Haystack drifted from 3.6x to 5.3x without changing a thing
body: Meta's Tectonic paper shows the IOPS-per-TB trap in real life. As drives grew larger, IOPS per TB declined and Haystack, the hot photo store, became IOPS-bound: its drives ran out of random-read capacity before they filled. Meta had to add drives just for IOPS, leaving capacity unused. That spare capacity pushed Haystack's effective replication factor, physical bytes per logical byte, from 3.6 up to 5.3, even though its replication scheme never changed.
deeper:
This is a subtle point worth internalizing: effective replication factor measures physical capacity purchased per logical byte, not just the number of copies. Empty space bought for performance counts. Haystack still stored 3 replicas on RAID-6 disks, but because disks sat partly empty for IOPS, each logical byte consumed 5.3 bytes of physical capacity.

The chapter's quiz answer summarizes the chain: drives grew bigger but IOPS per drive stayed flat, so IOPS per TB fell. Haystack needed extra drives just for IOPS, leaving capacity unused, which raised physical bytes per logical byte.

This failure mode is part of why Meta designed Tectonic as it did and why storage architects separate hot and cold data. Hot data belongs on media sized for IOPS, possibly flash; cold data belongs on the densest drives. Mixing them on one tier forces a compromise that is wrong for both, and the cost grows every drive generation.

quiz.q: How did Haystack's effective replication factor rise to 5.3x with no change to its replication scheme?
quiz.a: IOPS per TB fell as drives grew, making Haystack IOPS-bound. Extra drives bought for IOPS sat partly empty, raising physical bytes per logical byte.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
title: SMR drives: 10-20% more data, but writes must be sequential
body: SMR (shingled magnetic recording) drives overlap tracks like roof shingles to fit more data on each platter. The catch is that writes must be sequential within fixed zones, because rewriting one track would damage the overlapping neighbor. Dropbox was one of the first large companies to run SMR in production, starting September 2018. SMR gave roughly 10% to 20% more data per drive at similar cost, and the new design saved more than 20% overall versus the previous generation.
deeper:
Dropbox handled SMR's slow and restrictive writes by staging them on an SSD cache, then writing to the SMR drives sequentially in large chunks. SMR worked for Dropbox because its storage is mostly large, immutable blobs written sequentially, which matches SMR's constraints almost perfectly.

SMR sharpens the IOPS-per-TB trade: more capacity per drive with the same mechanical arm means even fewer IOPS per TB, and random writes are especially bad. A workload with frequent small updates or random writes would suffer badly on SMR.

The overall saving of more than 20% did not come from SMR alone. As covered earlier, Dropbox's 2018 design also increased density from 60 to 100 disks per machine with the same CPU and memory. The playbook lists denser drives and SMR as high effort (hardware and software changes), with dropping IOPS per TB as the risk, and cold, sequential blobs as the best first target.

quiz.q: Why is SMR a good fit for Dropbox but a poor fit for a database with random updates?
quiz.a: SMR requires sequential writes within zones. Dropbox stores large immutable blobs written sequentially (staged via SSD); random updates would conflict with overlapping tracks and collapse performance.

section: 12.4.2 The IOPS-per-TB trap: when bigger drives cost more
title: The right unit is the cheaper of $/TB and $/IOPS
body: Senior staff lens: the right unit for a storage decision is not dollars per TB. It is the cheaper of dollars per TB and dollars per IOPS for your specific workload. Cold archives are capacity-bound, so buy the biggest, densest drives available. Hot small-object stores are IOPS-bound, so big drives waste money and flash may be cheaper overall, even though flash costs several times more per TB. The binding constraint determines which price actually matters.
deeper:
To apply this, estimate both requirements: how many TB the data needs and how many IOPS its access pattern demands. Then compute how many devices of each type you would need to satisfy both. The device count is set by whichever constraint binds first, and cost follows.

For a cold archive, capacity binds: a few IOPS per TB is plenty, so the densest HDD minimizes devices. For a hot store of small objects such as user profiles or message indexes, IOPS binds: you might need many HDDs mostly empty, whereas a few SSDs would supply the IOPS with capacity to spare. At that point flash wins on total cost despite a higher sticker price per TB.

The key takeaway repeats this rule: choose media by the cheaper of dollars per TB and dollars per IOPS. Haystack's drift to 5.3x is the cautionary example of what happens when a hot workload is provisioned as if capacity were the only constraint.

quiz.q: Why might flash be cheaper overall than HDD for a hot small-object store despite costing more per TB?
quiz.a: The store is IOPS-bound; HDDs would need many mostly-empty drives to supply enough IOPS, while fewer SSDs meet the IOPS need, lowering total cost.

title: Flash vs disk: route data by what limits it
body: Flash costs more per TB than hard disk but gives orders of magnitude more IOPS per TB. The decision rule follows from that. Capacity-bound data, such as photos older than a month, data lake files and backups, belongs on HDD or even colder media. IOPS-bound data, such as user profiles, message indexes, metadata and hot small objects, belongs on flash. Mixed workloads use HDD for the bulk plus a flash cache or flash tier for the hot part.
deeper:
Real systems mostly land in the mixed case. Meta's Tectonic storage nodes each carry a 1 TB SSD used for metadata and for caching hot chunks, while the bulk data sits on hard drives. Google's Colossus places hot data on flash and moves it to disk as it ages.

The mixed approach exploits skew: a small fraction of data receives most of the accesses. Putting that fraction on flash satisfies the IOPS demand, letting the HDD tier be sized purely for capacity with the densest drives. It avoids both extremes: an all-flash system that overpays for capacity and an all-HDD system that must be overprovisioned for IOPS, like Haystack.

Metadata deserves special mention. It is small, read on almost every operation and randomly accessed, making it the classic IOPS-bound data. Keeping metadata on flash even in otherwise HDD-based systems is a common pattern because slow metadata slows every request.

The playbook's 'right media' lever is on the cheaper-bytes side of the lever tree.

quiz.q: Why do systems like Tectonic keep metadata on SSD even when bulk data is on HDD?
quiz.a: Metadata is small, randomly accessed and touched on nearly every operation, so it is IOPS-bound; flash serves it fast cheaply, while HDDs stay sized for bulk capacity.

title: Compression is often the cheapest lever: no hardware needed
body: Compression shrinks bytes with software alone, so it is often the cheapest cost lever. Zstandard (zstd), open-sourced by Facebook in 2016, compresses 3 to 5 times faster than zlib at the same ratio, or produces output 10% to 15% smaller at the same speed. Its current benchmark shows zstd level 1 reaching a 2.896 compression ratio against zlib level 1 at 2.743, with about 4 times faster decompression. Faster codecs make compression affordable in more places.
deeper:
Because compression needs no new drives, servers or datacenter space, it can be rolled out as a software change with quick payback. The playbook rates it as low effort, with CPU cost as the main risk, and logs and lake tables as the best first targets.

The trade-off is CPU on both write and read. The chapter gives a simple rule for choosing a compression level: for cold data, use a higher compression level, because you spend CPU once and save bytes for years. For hot data, use a fast level, because it is read and written often and CPU cost recurs on every access.

zstd's speed matters for this trade. If decompression is about 4 times faster than zlib, you can compress hot data that was previously too expensive to decompress on each read. The ratio numbers look modest, 2.896 versus 2.743 at level 1, but applied across petabytes, a few percent smaller output plus much lower CPU adds up to real money.

quiz.q: Why should cold data use a higher compression level than hot data?
quiz.a: Cold data is compressed once and stored for years, so extra CPU buys lasting byte savings; hot data is accessed often, so CPU cost recurs and a fast level is better.

title: Trained dictionaries lift small-record compression from 2.8x to 6.9x
body: Small records compress poorly because a compressor has little data in which to find repeated patterns. Dictionary compression fixes this: you train a dictionary on sample records, capturing common strings like field names, and both compressor and decompressor use it. Facebook's example of roughly 1 KB JSON records improved from a 2.8x compression ratio to 6.9x with a trained dictionary. This matters for the chapter's profile store, where each user profile record is small and similarly structured.
deeper:
The mechanism: general compressors learn patterns as they go, so on a 1 KB record they finish before learning much. A dictionary provides that knowledge upfront. Records sharing a schema, such as JSON with the same keys, benefit most because the repeated field names and typical values live in the dictionary instead of in every record.

More than doubling the ratio, from 2.8x to 6.9x, means storing less than half the bytes for the same data. For a store holding a billion small profiles, that is a large saving with no hardware change.

There are operational considerations. The dictionary must be stored and versioned, because every record compressed with it needs the same dictionary to decompress. If record structure drifts over time, the dictionary may need retraining, and old records must keep access to the old dictionary. zstd supports trained dictionaries, which is part of why Facebook highlighted this use case when it open-sourced the library in 2016.

quiz.q: Why does a trained dictionary help small records far more than large files?
quiz.a: Small records give the compressor too little data to learn repeated patterns; a dictionary supplies common strings like field names upfront, so each record needn't contain them.

title: Columnar formats compress far better than rows
body: Columnar file formats such as Parquet, ORC and Google's Capacitor store all values of one column together instead of storing records row by row. Values in one column are similar, such as all country codes or all timestamps, so they compress far better than mixed row data. Encodings like dictionary encoding and run-length encoding multiply the effect, and Capacitor goes further by reordering rows to group similar values. This makes columnar formats a major compression lever for analytics data.
deeper:
Dictionary encoding replaces repeated values with small integer codes, so a column with a few hundred distinct values costs a few bits per row. Run-length encoding stores a repeated value once plus a count, which works brilliantly when identical values sit next to each other. Row reordering, as Capacitor does, sorts or clusters rows so that more identical values become adjacent, making run-length encoding even more effective. Chapter 7 covered these techniques in detail.

General-purpose compression like zstd can then run on top of these encoded columns, compounding the saving.

The playbook lists compression as saving 10% to 15% over zlib with zstd, and more with columnar formats, at low effort and with CPU as the risk. Lake tables are one of the best first targets. The broader lesson: data layout drives compressibility. The same data stored as JSON rows and as sorted Parquet columns can differ enormously in size, without changing a single value.

quiz.q: Why does storing data by column compress better than storing it by row?
quiz.a: A column holds similar values, enabling dictionary and run-length encodings (amplified by row reordering), whereas rows mix unrelated types and values that compress poorly.

title: Deduplication: identical content stored once, by hash
body: Deduplication stores identical content only once. Content-addressed systems name each chunk of data by a hash of its content, so two identical uploads produce the same name and map to one stored chunk. The second upload simply adds a reference instead of new bytes. It works best when many users store the same files: shared attachments, forwarded videos, or backups of many similar machines. The playbook rates it medium effort, with savings that depend entirely on the duplicate rate.
deeper:
Content addressing makes duplicate detection automatic: computing the hash of incoming data and looking it up tells you instantly whether that content already exists. No comparison of full files is needed.

The benefit depends on how much duplication exists. A messaging app where one popular video is forwarded millions of times can save massively by storing it once. Backups of fleets of machines running the same operating system repeat most of their bytes. A dataset of unique user photos has little to deduplicate.

Deduplication also has limits and risks, covered next: it works poorly on already-compressed or encrypted data, and it creates a new deletion problem. The playbook's best first targets are backups and shared attachments, and its listed risk is blunt: garbage collection bugs lose data. Dedup should be reserved for datasets where measurements show a meaningful duplicate rate, since otherwise you pay its complexity and hashing cost for little saving.

quiz.q: How does content addressing make deduplication work?
quiz.a: Each chunk is named by a hash of its content, so identical data yields the same name; a duplicate upload maps to the existing chunk and only adds a reference.

title: Dedup's catch: encrypted data and deletion bugs
body: Deduplication works poorly on already-compressed or encrypted data, where identical content rarely produces identical bytes, so hashes do not match. It also creates a new problem: you cannot delete a chunk until no one references it anymore. That requires reference counting or garbage collection to track every user of each chunk. A bug in that bookkeeping can delete a chunk someone still needs, which means lost data. Dedup trades storage savings for correctness risk in deletion.
deeper:
Why compressed and encrypted data resists dedup: encryption is designed to make output look random, and different keys or settings produce different bytes for the same input. Compression can also shift byte boundaries so that small differences change everything downstream. Dedup must therefore happen before encryption or compression, or not at all.

The deletion problem is structural. Without dedup, deleting a file frees its bytes. With dedup, deleting one user's file must only decrement a reference; the chunk survives until the last reference goes. Reference counts can drift due to crashes or races, and garbage collectors that scan for unreferenced chunks can race with new uploads that just started referencing an old chunk.

The failure mode is asymmetric: a bug that leaks references merely wastes space, but a bug that under-counts references destroys data that users believe is safe. That is why the playbook lists 'GC bugs lose data' as dedup's risk and why dedup systems need extensive safety checks.

quiz.q: Why does deduplication make deletion risky?
quiz.a: A shared chunk can be removed only when no references remain, requiring reference counting or GC; any bug that under-counts references deletes data others still rely on.

section: 12.4.6 Retention hygiene: delete what you do not need
title: The cheapest byte is the one you delete
body: Retention hygiene means deleting data nobody needs. At most companies, a large share of stored bytes is waste: old table snapshots and versions no one will roll back to, orphan files left by failed jobs, staging and temp data with no TTL (time to live, an automatic expiry time), one-off dataset copies made for an analysis years ago, and old object versions in buckets with versioning turned on but no lifecycle rule for non-current versions.
deeper:
Each category grows silently. Table formats that keep snapshots for time travel accumulate old versions unless snapshots are expired. Failed jobs leave partial output that no table references, so nothing ever reads or deletes it. Temp data without a TTL outlives the job that created it. Analyst copies outlive the analyst's interest, and often the analyst's employment. Bucket versioning keeps every overwritten or deleted object as a non-current version, billed like any other data, unless a lifecycle rule expires them.

Deletion beats every other lever because it removes the bytes and all their multipliers: replicas, backups, tiering fees and energy. The key takeaways group retention hygiene with compression as the cheapest levers because neither needs new hardware.

The playbook rates deleting unused data and adding TTLs as high but variable savings at low to medium effort. The risk is deleting data someone actually needed, so the best first targets are the safest: temp and staging data and old snapshots.

quiz.q: Why can enabling bucket versioning without a lifecycle rule quietly inflate storage cost?
quiz.a: Every overwrite or delete keeps the old object as a non-current version that is billed like normal data, and without a lifecycle rule these versions never expire.

section: 12.4.6 Retention hygiene: delete what you do not need
title: Make retention a platform job with an owner
body: LinkedIn's OpenHouse, its table management platform, runs snapshot expiration, orphan file deletion and retention enforcement as platform jobs, precisely because leaving cleanup to individual teams does not work. The chapter's advice: treat retention like a feature with an owner, not a one-time cleanup project. Cleanup projects reclaim space once and then waste accumulates again. A platform that continuously enforces retention keeps waste from building up in the first place.
deeper:
The contrast is between episodic and continuous effort. A cleanup project gets staffed after someone notices the bill, spends weeks finding and deleting waste, declares victory, and disbands. Within a year the same categories of waste are back, because nothing changed in how data is created.

A platform approach builds retention into the system. Snapshot expiration runs on a schedule for every table. Orphan file deletion finds files no table references and removes them safely. Retention policies are declared per dataset and enforced centrally. Teams do not need to remember anything.

This connects to the FinOps senior staff lens later in the chapter: a storage efficiency program succeeds when the platform makes the cheap choice the default, with TTLs required on creation, lifecycle rules applied by default, compaction and retention run centrally, and owner names attached to large datasets. OpenHouse is a concrete example of that philosophy applied to lake tables.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter recommend platform-run retention jobs over periodic cleanup projects?
quiz.a: Cleanup projects reclaim space once, then waste regrows. Platform jobs like OpenHouse's snapshot expiry and orphan deletion enforce retention continuously without relying on teams.

title: For every copy, ask: which failure does this protect against?
body: Not every copy of data is needed. A common pattern of waste: a database with 3 replicas in every region, plus a backup, plus a data lake copy, plus a warm cache copy. For each copy, ask what failure it protects against and whether another copy already covers that failure. Meta's f4 is the model: it cut its effective replication factor from 3.6x to 2.1x by deciding carefully which failures (disk, host, rack, datacenter) each layer of redundancy covers.
deeper:
Copies accumulate because each is added by a different team for a different reason, and nobody sees the total. Regional replicas guard against zone and region failures. Backups guard against logical corruption and accidental deletion, which replicas faithfully copy. A lake copy serves analytics. A cache copy serves latency. Some of these are distinct needs; others overlap. Two disaster-recovery copies in different systems may protect against the same regional failure twice.

f4 shows the disciplined approach. Erasure coding inside a datacenter covers disk, host and rack failures. The cross-datacenter XOR covers datacenter loss. No layer duplicates another's job, so no capacity is spent twice.

The playbook rates right-sizing replicas as low effort, saving one copy for each extra replica removed, with lower durability as the risk if you remove a copy that was the only protection against some failure. Best first targets are duplicate disaster-recovery and lake copies, where overlap is most common.

quiz.q: Why might a backup be necessary even when data already has 3 replicas in each region?
quiz.a: Replicas protect against hardware and site failures but faithfully copy corruption or accidental deletion; a backup covers those logical failures, which replicas do not.

title: Cloud usually wins until your scale is huge and steady
body: A cloud storage price includes the provider's hardware, power, staff and profit margin. At small and medium scale, the cloud is almost always cheaper than running your own storage once you count the people needed to operate it. At very large and steady scale, owning hardware (on-prem) can win because you stop paying the provider's margin on a huge, predictable base. Real companies have gone both ways, and scale alone does not decide.
deeper:
The logic follows from TCO. Running storage yourself requires a team to design, deploy, operate and replace hardware, which is a large fixed cost. At small scale that fixed cost dwarfs any saving on hardware versus cloud prices. As scale grows, hardware and power dominate and the fixed team cost is spread thin, so the provider's margin becomes the big number you could save.

Predictability matters as much as size. Clouds let you pay for what you use and grow instantly. Owning means buying capacity ahead of demand; if growth is spiky or uncertain, you either overbuy and waste money or underbuy and run out.

The chapter presents three real cases: Dropbox moving off AWS S3 onto its own system, 37signals leaving S3 in 2025 despite being a modest-size company, and Uber moving the other way from its own Hadoop datacenters to Google Cloud. Together they show the decision depends on scale, steadiness, egress, team, speed and capital, not just price.

quiz.q: Why is the cloud usually cheaper at small scale even though its price includes the provider's margin?
quiz.a: Running your own storage needs a team and fixed operations cost; at small scale that outweighs the margin you would save, which only dominates at large steady scale.

title: Dropbox's Magic Pocket saved about $74.6M in two years
body: Dropbox built its own storage system, Magic Pocket, and by October 2015 had moved about 90% of user data onto it from AWS S3. At that time the system held over 500 PB. In its 2018 IPO filing, Dropbox reported that this 'Infrastructure Optimization' saved about $39.5 million in 2016 over 2015, and a further $35.1 million in 2017, about $74.6 million over two years. Dropbox still used AWS for a small part of its storage.
deeper:
Dropbox fits every factor that favors owning storage. Its storage is its core product, so storage cost is central to its business. Its data was very large and growing steadily and predictably. It could hire and keep a strong storage engineering team. And its data, mostly large immutable blobs, suited cost-optimized hardware like the SMR drives and 100-disk servers it later deployed.

The chapter's quiz answer summarizes why Dropbox chose differently from Uber: Dropbox's storage was its core product, very large, steady and predictable, and it could build a storage team.

Note that Dropbox did not leave the cloud completely. Keeping a small part on AWS gave flexibility where owning made less sense. This hybrid approach is common: move the large, stable base onto owned hardware, keep spiky or specialized needs in the cloud.

The savings figures come from the company's official IPO filing, which makes this one of the best-documented cloud exit cases available.

quiz.q: What made Dropbox a strong candidate to leave AWS S3 for its own storage?
quiz.a: Storage was its core product, at very large, steady, predictable scale, and it could build and keep a storage team, so avoiding the provider's margin paid off.

title: 37signals left S3 in 2025 and projected about $5M saved
body: 37signals, maker of Basecamp and HEY, left Amazon S3 in 2025. It said it paid just under $1.5 million per year for S3. It bought about 18 PB of Pure Storage capacity across two datacenters for about $1.5 million, with support costing under $1 million over five years, and projected savings of nearly $5 million over five years. AWS offered a free 60-day egress window to move about 6 PB of data out.
deeper:
This case is useful because 37signals is not a giant like Dropbox or Meta. Its savings came from very steady, predictable storage and a team willing to run hardware, not from exabyte scale. It shows that the threshold for on-prem economics is less about raw size and more about stability and operational willingness.

The numbers are simple to follow: roughly one year's S3 bill buys the hardware, and five years of support costs under $1 million. Against about $7.5 million of S3 spending over five years, that projects nearly $5 million in savings.

The egress detail matters. Moving petabytes out of a cloud can cost a fortune in egress fees, which acts as a barrier to leaving. AWS's free 60-day egress window removed that one-time cost for about 6 PB. Any migration plan must account for egress and for the time limit: a free window that expires turns a migration delay into a real bill.

quiz.q: Why is 37signals an instructive case even though it is much smaller than Dropbox?
quiz.a: It shows on-prem can win without huge scale when storage is very steady and predictable and the team is willing to run hardware.

title: Uber went the other way: 1+ EB per region to Google Cloud
body: In 2024 Uber announced it would move its batch data platform, with more than 1 exabyte in each of two regions, from its own Hadoop datacenters to Google Cloud, starting with Google Cloud Storage as the data lake. That is enormous, steady scale, exactly where owning hardware supposedly wins. Uber valued faster access to managed services and less datacenter work over the savings of owning. Scale alone does not decide the cloud versus on-prem answer.
deeper:
Uber's move is the counterexample that keeps the cloud versus on-prem debate honest. If size were the only factor, Uber would never leave its own datacenters. Instead it weighed other things: access to managed services that let teams build faster, and freeing engineers from running datacenter operations.

The chapter's quiz contrasts it with Dropbox: Dropbox's storage was its core product, very large, steady and predictable, and it could build a storage team. Uber valued managed services and less datacenter operations, and its cost was spread over a broader data platform rather than being the core product itself.

The key takeaway puts the three cases together: owning storage can win at large, steady scale (Dropbox saved about $74.6 million over two years, 37signals projects about $5 million over five years), but Uber shows large companies also move to the cloud for speed and managed services. Cost is one input; strategic focus is another.

quiz.q: Give two reasons Uber moved its lake to the cloud while Dropbox left it.
quiz.a: Uber valued managed services and less datacenter operations, and storage was not its core product; Dropbox's storage was its core, steady, predictable product with a capable storage team.

title: Six factors that tip the cloud vs on-prem decision
body: Six factors decide whether cloud or on-prem storage fits. Scale: small or fast-changing favors cloud; large and steady, many PB, favors on-prem. Growth: unpredictable, spiky growth favors cloud; predictable, plannable growth favors on-prem. Egress: low, or data staying in cloud, favors cloud; high egress to users or partners favors on-prem. Team: no storage hardware team favors cloud. Speed: needing new services quickly favors cloud. Capital: preferring operating expense favors cloud; spending capital upfront favors on-prem.
deeper:
The factors interact. A company with many petabytes but spiky growth may still prefer the cloud because it cannot plan hardware purchases. A company with steady data but no ability to hire a storage team faces operational risk that erases paper savings.

The team factor is subtle: it is not just hiring, but keeping a team long term. On-prem storage is a multi-year commitment; losing expertise midway is dangerous.

The speed factor reflects what Uber valued: the cloud offers managed services immediately, while on-prem suits a stable, well-known workload where you rarely need something new.

Capital reflects finance: on-prem means large upfront hardware purchases (capital expense), while cloud spreads cost as monthly operating expense.

The chapter adds a decision flow. Under 1 PB or unpredictable: stay in cloud and optimize tiers. Many PB, steady growth, high egress: ask if you can build and run a storage team; if no, negotiate committed-use discounts; if yes, model 5-year on-prem TCO.

quiz.q: Why does heavy egress to users favor on-prem storage?
quiz.a: Cloud egress is billed per GB at high rates, so heavy internet serving inflates cloud bills, while owned infrastructure avoids per-GB egress pricing.

title: Decision flow: when to even consider leaving the cloud
body: The chapter's decision flow starts with scale. If storage is under 1 PB or unpredictable, stay in the cloud and optimize tiers. If you have many PB, steady growth and high egress, ask: can you build and run a storage team? If not, negotiate cloud committed-use discounts. If yes, model on-prem TCO over 5 years. If the savings are still large after counting people and risk, consider a migration like Dropbox or 37signals; if not, negotiate discounts instead.
deeper:
The flow is deliberately conservative. Migration is only reached after passing three gates: scale and stability, team capability, and a full TCO model where savings survive people and risk. Every 'no' leads back to optimizing within the cloud, either through tiering or through committed-use discounts, where you commit to a spending level in exchange for lower prices.

The 5-year horizon matches typical hardware lifetimes, like the 5-year drive life used in the usable-TB example, so the model captures a full hardware cycle including refresh.

'Risk' in the final gate includes the migration itself: moving petabytes takes time, engineering effort and egress fees, and something can go wrong. 37signals mitigated one part of this with AWS's free 60-day egress window.

The flow also shows that negotiating is itself a lever. A credible on-prem TCO model strengthens your hand in discount negotiations even if you never migrate. For most companies, the right answer is staying in the cloud and optimizing.

quiz.q: In the decision flow, what should a large, steady company do if it cannot build and run a storage team?
quiz.a: Stay in the cloud and negotiate committed-use discounts, since on-prem savings depend on having a capable team to operate the hardware.

title: Common mistake: cloud list price vs drive cost
body: A common mistake in the cloud versus on-prem debate is comparing the cloud's list price with the cost of drives. That comparison flatters on-prem enormously, because drives are a minority of TCO and list prices ignore discounts. The fair comparison is the cloud price after negotiated discounts against the full on-prem TCO: hardware, spares, power, space, network, people, and the risk and time of the migration itself.
deeper:
Both sides of the naive comparison are wrong. On the cloud side, large customers rarely pay list prices; negotiated and committed-use discounts can cut the price significantly, as the worked example's blended $0.05 per GB egress rate suggests. On the on-prem side, drives are one line of six. Servers, redundancy, fill headroom, spares for failed hardware, power and cooling, datacenter space, network and a staff to run it all can multiply the drive cost several times.

The migration itself is a real cost: engineering months, parallel running of both systems, egress fees to move data out, and the risk of data loss or downtime during the move.

This mistake mirrors the senior staff lens from the start of the chapter: always check whether a cost per TB is raw or usable, which redundancy, what fill level, and whether it includes power, space and people. A drive-versus-list-price comparison fails all four questions at once and can overstate on-prem savings many times over.

quiz.q: What is the fair way to compare cloud and on-prem storage cost?
quiz.a: Compare the cloud price after negotiated discounts with full on-prem TCO: hardware, spares, power, space, network, people, plus migration risk and time.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: FinOps: make engineers own their cloud cost
body: FinOps (financial operations) is the practice of making engineering teams responsible for their cloud cost, rather than leaving it to finance to discover on an invoice. The FinOps Foundation describes the work in three repeating phases: Inform (see the cost), Optimize (reduce it), and Operate (make it continuous). For storage, the key practices are tagging, showback and chargeback, storage analytics tools, quotas and unit cost metrics. Together they turn cost into an ongoing engineering discipline.
deeper:
The three phases form a loop, not a one-time project. Inform means making cost visible: who owns which data, how much it costs, and how it is used. Without visibility there is nothing to optimize. Optimize applies the levers: tiering, deletion, compression, right-sizing replicas. Operate makes the improvements stick through policies, defaults, budgets and ongoing monitoring, so cost does not creep back.

The chapter's FinOps flow for storage runs: tag every bucket and table with an owner, collect usage and access metadata, build showback dashboards per team, find waste such as no-access data, orphan files and missing TTLs, apply fixes like tiering, deletion and compression, and finally use chargeback and quotas to keep it fixed.

The underlying idea is accountability. Engineers make the decisions that drive cost, such as data formats, retention, replication and access patterns. If they never see the cost, they cannot weigh it. FinOps puts cost next to latency and reliability as something engineers measure and manage.

quiz.q: What are the FinOps Foundation's three phases, and why do they repeat?
quiz.a: Inform, Optimize, Operate. They repeat because data and usage keep changing; visibility, fixes and enforcement must continue or costs creep back.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: No tag, no owner: tagging is step one of storage FinOps
body: Tagging means every bucket, volume and table carries tags naming its owner team, service and environment, such as production or staging. Without tags, no one owns the cost: a huge bucket with no clear owner cannot be charged to anyone, questioned, or safely deleted.
