Tagging is the foundation for every other FinOps practice, because showback, chargeback, quotas and waste hunting all depend on knowing whose data is whose. It is the first step in the chapter's storage FinOps flow.
deeper:
Untagged storage is a classic source of waste. A dataset created years ago by someone who has since changed teams sits on the bill indefinitely because nobody knows whether it is safe to delete. With tags, the question 'who owns this 2 PB bucket?' has an answer, and that owner can decide.

The environment tag matters because non-production data often has different retention needs. Staging and test data should usually expire; production data may need long retention. Tags let policies differ by environment.

For tagging to work, it must be enforced at creation, not added later. Retroactive tagging projects are painful and incomplete. The chapter's senior staff lens on FinOps calls for printing the owner's name next to every large dataset, which is only possible with reliable tags.

Inside large companies, the same function is often served by metadata tables listing every file's size, owner, age and last access time. Whether cloud tags or internal metadata, the principle is the same: every byte needs a known owner.

quiz.q: Why is tagging a prerequisite for showback, chargeback and waste cleanup?
quiz.a: All of them need to know who owns each dataset; without owner tags, cost cannot be reported or billed to a team, and nobody can decide whether data is safe to delete.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: Showback builds awareness; chargeback changes behavior
body: Showback reports each team's storage cost to that team, so they can see it. Chargeback goes further and actually bills the cost to the team's budget. Showback builds awareness: teams learn what their data costs. Chargeback changes behavior, because real money leaves their budget, but it needs accurate data or teams will fight the numbers. That is why many companies start with showback and move to chargeback once cost data is trusted. The playbook rates both as behavioral, lasting savings.
deeper:
The chapter's quiz answer explains the sequencing: companies start with showback because tagging and cost data must be accurate and trusted before money moves between budgets. If a team is charged for data it does not own, or at a cost it cannot verify, the conversation becomes a dispute about the numbers instead of a decision about the data.

Showback is lower stakes, which makes it a good way to debug the data. Teams reviewing showback dashboards spot mis-tagged resources and incorrect allocations. Once those are fixed and the numbers are credible, chargeback can switch on.

Chargeback's power comes from aligning incentives. When a team's own budget pays for its storage, retention policies, compression and tiering become that team's priorities.

The playbook groups showback, chargeback and quotas as a medium-effort lever whose saving is behavioral and lasting, with team friction as the main risk. The best first target is all teams, because the goal is organization-wide cost awareness.

quiz.q: Why do many companies start with showback before moving to chargeback?
quiz.a: Chargeback moves real money, so tagging and cost data must be accurate and trusted first; otherwise teams dispute the numbers instead of fixing their storage.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: S3 Storage Lens and metadata tables reveal the waste
body: Storage analytics tools show where bytes and money go. AWS S3 Storage Lens gives 62 free metrics at bucket level with 14 days of history. Paid advanced metrics add prefix-level views, 15 months of history and organization-wide views across thousands of accounts. Similar tools exist on other clouds. Inside big companies, the same job is done with metadata tables listing every file's size, owner, age and last access time, which can then be queried to find waste.
deeper:
Analytics tools power the Inform phase of FinOps and the waste-finding step of the storage flow. The questions they answer are practical: which buckets grew most this month, which prefixes have not been read in a year, which datasets lack lifecycle rules, which teams own the most cold data.

The difference between free and paid tiers matters. Bucket-level metrics with 14 days of history show current state but not long-term trends. Prefix-level views reveal which part of a bucket is responsible, often necessary because one bucket may hold data from many sources. Fifteen months of history lets you see seasonal patterns and verify that optimizations stuck.

Internal metadata tables are the large-company equivalent: a table with one row per file, including last access time, lets engineers write simple queries like 'all files owned by team X, larger than 1 TB, not read in 180 days'. That turns waste hunting from guesswork into a report, and it provides the measured access data needed to choose tiering safely.

quiz.q: Why is last access time an especially valuable field in storage metadata tables?
quiz.a: It identifies data nobody reads, the prime candidates for deletion or colder tiers, and supplies the measured access data needed to tier safely.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: Quotas force the conversation before growth, not after
body: Per-team storage quotas cap how much a team can store. They force a conversation before growth happens, rather than after a surprising bill arrives. Uber used namespace quotas as part of controlling the small-files problem in its HDFS clusters. The companion practice is unit cost metrics: track cost per user, per photo, or per TB served, not only total cost. Total cost naturally rises with growth, while unit cost shows whether efficiency is really improving.
deeper:
Quotas change the timing of cost decisions. Without them, a team can grow its storage indefinitely and cost only becomes visible after the fact. With them, exceeding a quota triggers a request, which prompts questions: is this growth expected, can old data be deleted first, is there a cheaper tier? The playbook groups quotas with showback and chargeback as the practices that keep fixes in place.

Uber's example shows quotas also limit harmful patterns, not just bytes. HDFS stores metadata for every file in memory on its NameNode, so millions of tiny files strain the system. Namespace quotas limit file counts and push teams to consolidate small files.

Unit cost metrics solve a communication problem. A growing company's storage bill rises every year; alone, that looks like failure. But if cost per user or per photo falls, efficiency is improving even as the business grows. Conversely, flat total cost with shrinking usage would hide worsening efficiency. Unit cost is the metric that shows whether engineering work is actually paying off.

quiz.q: Why track unit cost metrics like cost per photo instead of only total storage cost?
quiz.a: Total cost rises naturally with growth, masking progress; unit cost shows whether efficiency is actually improving independent of business growth.

section: 12.6 FinOps: running storage cost as a discipline
title: Efficiency programs fail on memory, succeed on defaults
body: Senior staff lens: a storage efficiency program fails if it depends on each team remembering to clean up. It succeeds when the platform makes the cheap choice the default. That means TTLs are required when data is created, lifecycle rules are applied by default, compaction and retention run centrally, and the owner's name is printed next to every large dataset. Good defaults keep waste from accumulating without anyone needing to think about it.
deeper:
The reasoning is about human behavior at scale. Across hundreds of teams, some will always forget, be too busy, or move on. A system that relies on voluntary cleanup accumulates waste at the rate of the least careful team. A system with good defaults makes waste the exception that requires active effort.

Each default targets a waste category from the retention hygiene section. Required TTLs prevent staging and temp data from living forever. Default lifecycle rules handle non-current object versions and tier cooling data automatically. Central compaction and retention, as LinkedIn's OpenHouse does, remove old snapshots and orphan files without per-team work. Showing the owner's name next to large datasets creates social accountability: it is harder to ignore a 5 PB dataset with your name on it.

This lens ties the whole chapter together. The levers work, but only if they are applied continuously, and the only reliable way to apply them continuously across an organization is to build them into the platform.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter say efficiency programs should rely on platform defaults rather than team discipline?
quiz.a: Across many teams some will always forget; defaults like required TTLs, automatic lifecycle rules and central retention prevent waste without relying on memory.

title: Storage energy: keeping data vs serving data
body: Storage energy has two parts. The energy to keep data covers spinning drives, powered servers and cooling, paid every hour whether or not anyone reads the data. The energy to serve data covers reads, rebuilds and scrubbing (periodically reading data to detect errors). For cold data, the keep part dominates, because it is rarely read. So the biggest energy wins for cold data come from media that uses no power at rest, such as tape.
deeper:
This split mirrors the cost split between storage and access in a cloud bill. Hot data spends significant energy serving requests. Cold data spends almost all its energy just existing: platters spinning, servers powered, fans running, all for bytes that may not be read for months.

That is why energy efficiency for cold storage focuses on reducing the power drawn at rest. Options include denser drives, which put more TB behind each watt; powering down drives that are not in use; and media such as tape and glass, which draw no power while stored.

The chapter adds that the efficiency levers already discussed are also sustainability levers. Every byte deleted, compressed or erasure-coded instead of replicated is a byte that no drive has to spin for. A move from 3x replication to 1.4x erasure coding cuts energy for keeping that data by more than half, just as it cuts hardware cost. Cost efficiency and energy efficiency point in the same direction.

quiz.q: Why do energy savings for cold data focus on media that uses no power at rest?
quiz.a: Cold data is rarely read, so nearly all its energy goes to keeping it (spinning drives, servers, cooling); eliminating power at rest removes the dominant part.

title: Meta's cold storage used under one-sixth of normal power
body: Meta's cold storage datacenters used less than one-sixth of the power of a normal Meta datacenter. Cold storage racks used about one-quarter of the power of normal storage servers, because only one drive per tray spun at a time. Tape uses no power at all while a cartridge sits in its library slot. Microsoft Research's Project Silica stores data in glass that needs no power at rest and no periodic refresh; it is still a research project.
deeper:
Meta's approach shows how far you can go with ordinary hard drives by designing for cold access. Keeping only one drive per tray spinning at a time accepts slower access, since reading a sleeping drive means waiting for it to spin up, in exchange for a large power cut. For data that is rarely read, that latency is acceptable.

Tape takes the idea to the extreme: cartridges sit unpowered on shelves, and a robot loads one into a drive only when needed. Retrieval takes much longer, but energy at rest is zero.

Project Silica goes further in another dimension. Magnetic media, both disk and tape, needs scrubbing: periodically reading data to detect and repair degradation, and eventually migrating to fresh media. Glass needs no periodic refresh and removes the energy spent scrubbing magnetic media. Because it is still research, it is not a lever you can deploy today, but it shows where archival storage may head.

All three trade access speed for energy, which suits truly cold data.

quiz.q: How did Meta's cold storage racks cut power to about one-quarter of normal storage servers?
quiz.a: Only one drive per tray spun at a time; the rest stayed powered down, trading slower access for much lower power, acceptable for rarely read data.

title: A 24 TB drive uses about 6x less energy per TB than a 4 TB
body: A back-of-envelope estimate with assumptions: a hard drive uses about 8 watts while spinning, regardless of capacity. A 4 TB drive therefore uses about 2 watts per TB, while a 24 TB drive uses about 0.33 watts per TB. Denser drives cut energy per TB about 6 times, before counting server and cooling savings. That is one more reason to fill cold tiers with the biggest drives and move truly cold data to media that can be powered off.
deeper:
The same physics that creates the IOPS-per-TB trap creates this energy win. A drive's power, like its IOPS, depends mostly on its motor and arm, not its capacity. So as capacity grows, both IOPS per TB and watts per TB fall. For hot data, falling IOPS per TB is a problem; for cold data, falling watts per TB is pure benefit.

The saving compounds beyond the drive. Fewer drives for the same data means fewer servers, fewer racks and less cooling, since cooling energy scales with the heat produced. The chapter notes the 6x figure is before counting these.

This connects the sustainability section to the media decision rule. Cold, capacity-bound data should sit on the densest drives for both cost and energy reasons. Data that is colder still should move to tape or other media that can be powered off entirely. The key takeaway summarizes it: energy per TB falls with denser drives and powered-off media, and deleting and compressing data are also sustainability wins.

quiz.q: Why do denser drives reduce energy per TB for cold data?
quiz.a: Drive power (about 8 W assumed) barely depends on capacity, so a larger drive spreads the same watts over more TB, e.g. 0.33 W/TB at 24 TB versus 2 W/TB at 4 TB.

title: Playbook: start with deletion, tiering and compression
body: The chapter's cost-optimization playbook ranks levers by saving, effort and risk. The easiest high-value levers come first. Deleting unused data and adding TTLs: high but variable saving, low to medium effort, risk of deleting needed data, best first on temp, staging and old snapshots. Lifecycle tiering: often more than half of storage cost for cold data, low effort, risks of retrieval fees and minimum durations, best on logs, old media and backups. Compression: 10% to 15% over zlib, more with columnar, low effort, CPU risk.
deeper:
Two related tiering entries differ in mechanism. Lifecycle tiering moves objects on fixed rules, such as after 90 days. Access-based tiering, like S3 Intelligent-Tiering, moves objects based on observed access, giving similar savings without retrieval fees and with very low effort. Its risks are a monitoring fee and that small objects are ignored, and it suits data with mixed or unknown access patterns.

Compression's best first targets are logs and lake tables, which are large, compressible and often stored in formats that can switch codecs or move to columnar layout.

The reason to start here is payback. These levers need no hardware, little engineering and can be rolled out quickly, so their payback periods are short. The senior staff lens on payback applies: under 3 months is an easy yes, and most of these qualify.

The risks are real but manageable: verify data is truly unneeded before deleting, model retrieval fees and object sizes before tiering, and choose compression levels by data temperature.

quiz.q: When would access-based tiering be preferable to lifecycle tiering?
quiz.a: When access patterns are mixed or unknown: it moves objects by observed use without retrieval fees, though it charges a monitoring fee and ignores small objects.

title: Playbook: platform-scale levers need real engineering
body: Some levers save a lot but require major platform or hardware work. Erasure coding instead of 3x replication cuts overhead from 3x to 1.33x to 1.67x, at high effort, with rebuild network and CPU as the risk; best for large sealed files. Denser drives and SMR saved Dropbox more than 20%, at high hardware and software effort, with falling IOPS per TB as the risk; best for cold, sequential blobs. Deduplication saves depending on duplicate rate, medium effort, but GC bugs can lose data.
deeper:
Other medium-effort levers fill out the middle of the table. Compaction merges small files into large ones, giving fewer requests and better compression, at the risk of write amplification, the extra writes caused by rewriting data; its best target is streaming lake tables. Right-sizing replicas removes one copy's cost per extra replica, at low effort, with lower durability as the risk; best on duplicate disaster-recovery and lake copies. Deduplication's best targets are backups and shared attachments.

The common thread is that these levers touch correctness or performance. Erasure coding changes how data survives failures. SMR changes write patterns. Dedup changes deletion semantics. Compaction rewrites live data. Each needs careful engineering and testing, which is why the payback period includes real engineering time.

These are the levers behind the big industry papers: f4 and Tectonic for erasure coding, Dropbox for SMR. At exabyte scale, the effort is justified many times over; at small scale, the simpler levers usually come first.

quiz.q: Why are erasure coding and SMR rated high effort even though their savings are large?
quiz.a: They change core platform behavior: erasure coding alters failure recovery, network and CPU use; SMR requires sequential writes and new hardware and software. Both need serious engineering.

title: Playbook: traffic and behavior levers finish the job
body: The last playbook levers target traffic and people rather than bytes. Reducing egress with a CDN gives large savings for media at medium effort, with cache misses as the risk; best for photos and videos. Avoiding cross-zone chatter can save more than the disk cost at medium effort, with lower zone isolation as the risk; best for self-managed replicated databases. Showback, chargeback and quotas give behavioral, lasting savings at medium effort, with team friction as the risk; they apply to all teams.
deeper:
These levers address bill lines that engineers most often overlook. Egress and cross-zone traffic do not appear as storage in engineers' mental models, yet the chapter shows each can dominate in the right workload: egress for a video streaming service, cross-zone transfer for a write-heavy self-managed database.

The behavioral levers work differently from technical ones. They do not directly remove bytes; they make teams care about bytes, so the other levers get applied continuously. Their saving is described as lasting precisely because it changes how data is created and retained, not just how existing data is stored.

Taken together, the playbook maps to the chapter's structure: understand true cost, read the bill line by line, apply the fewer-bytes and cheaper-bytes levers where payback is shortest, consider ownership only at large steady scale, and run it all as a continuous FinOps discipline with good platform defaults. Every lever that removes bytes also saves energy, making cost work and sustainability work the same work.

quiz.q: Why are behavioral levers like showback and quotas described as giving lasting savings?
quiz.a: They change how teams create and retain data going forward, so technical fixes stay applied instead of waste regrowing after one-off cleanups.
